names.name: Buttermilk bar
names.said: Split down the middle like it fell apart, which is how you know it is the right one.

text.what: Cake batter cut in a bar rather than a ring, fried so it splits open along the top, and glazed heavily enough that the glaze runs into the split.
text.story:
*Tradition holds —* the bar is a West Coast case staple and a test of a cake bench: too warm a batter and it will not crack, too cold and it breaks apart. It belongs to the same family as the old-fashioned, which cracks for the same reason, and shops that make a good one tend to make a good old-fashioned too.

No published history names an inventor or a first shop, and this project has not found one.
text.how: Buttermilk cake batter, rested cold, cut in rectangles, fried at a temperature low enough that the crust sets before the lift finishes. Glaze while warm.
text.today: Priced as a bar rather than a ring in most shops, which is to say a little more.

kin.as: Cracks for the same reason, in a ring.
A fixture of the California dozen.

text.story.note: no published origin found for the bar; the record says so rather than filling the gap
